title: Isolation of Melanopsin and Rhodopsin in the Human Eye Using Silent Substitution
author: Nugent, Carter, et al.
materials: Timing: 30–60 min per participant per step

steps.title: Define photoreceptor‑directed stimulus
steps.instruction: Specify the photoreceptor‑directed stimulus light for the experimental condition. With five photoreceptor classes in the eye, create five unique single‑photoreceptor stimuli that modulate only one opsin while the others remain silent (e.g., melanopsin‑directed). Also define post‑receptoral stimuli such as parvocellular (+L‑M), koniocellular (S‑cone), and magnocellular (+L+M luminance or +L+M+S achromatic). Combination stimuli (e.g., melanopsin and rhodopsin together) may be used with constant LMS excitation.

steps.title: Prepare silent‑substitution protocol
steps.instruction: Complete the five prerequisite actions before running silent substitution: (1) choose primary lights; (2) develop a display capable of presenting the photoreceptor‑directed stimuli; (3) calibrate the display; (4) perform individual observer calibrations; (5) confirm that silent substitution has been achieved.

steps.title: Confirm photoreceptor isolation
steps.instruction: Validate that the generated stimulus isolates the intended photoreceptor using at least one of the following methods (30–60 min per participant per step).

substeps.instruction: Color matching: Alternate a photoreceptor‑directed reference light (rod or melanopsin) with cone‑directed test lights adjustable along L/(L+M), S/(L+M) and (L+M). For melanopsin‑directed lights, apply temporal white noise (TWN) during inter‑stimulus intervals to suppress penumbral cone intrusion. Have the observer adjust cone excitations until the test light perceptually matches the reference. The equivalent cone signals are: (i) Mesopic rod percept – increment in S/(L+M) and (L+M) and decrement in L/(L+M); (ii) Photopic melanopsin percept – increment in cone luminance (L+M) and decrement in S/(L+M).

Critical Flicker Frequency (CFF): Generate cone‑, rhodopsin‑, and melanopsin‑directed stimuli using the A′‑matrix with individual observer corrections and apply TWN in inter‑stimulus intervals. Measure CFF for each stimulus by the method of adjustment; repeat rod‑directed measurements under scotopic and photopic illumination. Expected maximum CFF values are: cone‑directed (LMS) > 60 Hz; rod‑directed ≈ 30 Hz; melanopsin‑directed ≈ 5 Hz. Note that CFF depends on stimulus size, contrast, eccentricity and illumination level; open‑field errors will shift melanopsin or rhodopsin CFF toward cone CFF.

Bleach recovery test: (a) Dark‑adapt the participant for 15 min. (b) Generate separate cone‑, rhodopsin‑, and melanopsin‑directed stimuli with the A′‑matrix and apply TWN. (c) Pre‑expose one eye to a high‑intensity lamp (e.g., 70 s of 120 000 Photopic Td / 297 600 Scotopic Troland bleaching light) filtered to remove blue‑light hazard. (d) Estimate photopigment bleach levels using the Hollins & Alpern and Thomas & Lamb frameworks. (e) At time 0 (immediately after bleaching light offset) present suprathreshold photoreceptor‑directed pedestal stimuli periodically for ≈ 15 min or until detection, recording detection times. (f) Compare recovery times: cone pathway recovers fastest, rod slowest, melanopsin intermediate. Beware that bleaching narrows spectral nomograms and can introduce time‑dependent errors; longer post‑bleach intervals reduce these artefacts.

Entopic percept test: Present a melanopsin‑directed stimulus that strongly activates penumbral cones (e.g., a 10 Hz temporal grating). Ask the observer to grade the visibility of the retinal blood‑vessel (Purkinje) tree on a four‑point scale (0 = no structure, 1 = any structure, 2 = faint tree, 3 = strong tree). Presence of a graded Purkinje tree indicates penumbral cone intrusion.

steps.title: Pre‑experiment preparation
steps.instruction: Complete the following tasks (≈ 1 day, excluding institutional approvals): (1) Obtain all required institutional research‑ethics approvals. (2) Document participant demographics and clinical characteristics to enable replication: state recruitment method, inclusion/exclusion criteria for healthy and disease groups (including any ophthalmic/medical examinations), randomisation details, age, sex, ocular/systemic disease status, sleep or mood disorders, genotypes, etc.; list clinical instruments (model and manufacturer) used for visual acuity, contrast sensitivity, colour vision, fundus photography, OCT, intra‑ocular pressure, grading scales, medication documentation; perform a power analysis or other sample‑size determination based on the experimental design.

steps.title: Adapt participants to darkness
steps.instruction: Darken the laboratory. Have each observer sit in a dark‑room for 15 min before any test sessions to eliminate prior indoor or outdoor illumination. For rod‑mediated experiments, extend dark adaptation to 30–40 min depending on pre‑light exposure, then provide a pre‑adaptation to the background field (e.g., 2 min exposure to a 2000 Ph Td / 4360 Sc Td adapting field).

steps.title: Determine pre‑adaptation duration
steps.instruction: Run pilot experiments to find the optimal pre‑adaptation time that yields maximal sensitivity for all photoreceptor pathways. Verify that rods are not saturated under the chosen light levels using additional psychophysical, pupillographic, or electrophysiological measurements.

steps.title: Report laboratory measurement conditions
steps.instruction: Record and report: room illumination in lux; any pre‑dark or pre‑light adaptation duration (or lack thereof); background adaptation stimulus levels (scotopic, mesopic, photopic); environmental variables such as time‑of‑day, temperature, and humidity.

steps.title: Explain observer tasks and randomization
steps.instruction: Provide participants with clear instructions for all experimental tasks, including any observer calibration procedures. Randomise the order of stimulus presentation to minimise fatigue and learning effects. Allow sufficient practice trials, but exclude practice data from analysis.

description: The preliminary steps presented above are crucial to generating a truly photoreceptor-directed stimulus. The method of silent substitution can be applied under a wide range of experimental conditions107 once it has been confirmed that the generated stimulus is isolating the response of a single photoreceptor class. What follows in this section is an exemplar melanopsin-directed silent substitution experiment which puts together a selection of the preliminary steps discussed above and applies it to a melanopsin-directed temporal grating stimulus with temporal white noise in the inter-stimulus interval. A toolbox has been developed in MS-Excel to support this protocol and is available for download via the QUT Research Data Finder.11
